first: Paper changeover sheets are a waste

facts.problem: We write the same six values on a paper sheet at every changeover and then type them into the MES again.
facts.context: On all three lines of the 4-series, about twelve changeovers per shift, since the MES came in two years ago.
facts.evidence: I timed it last week: the paper part takes about five minutes per changeover.
facts.impact: That is about an hour per shift per line, so roughly 15 hours a week across the lines, plus typos we fix later.
facts.solution: Let the operator enter the values once on the line tablet, straight into the MES, and drop the paper sheet.
facts.risks: Quality wants a paper trail for audits, so the MES record would have to count as the audit record.
facts.success_measure: Changeover time down by five minutes and zero typed-twice values within a month.

first: New colleagues wait weeks before they can log into anything

facts.problem: New hires get their MES and ERP logins two to five weeks after they start, so they cannot book their own work.
facts.context: Every new hire in production, about two a month; tickets are raised one system at a time after the start date.
facts.evidence: Our last two apprentices started on 18 August and still had no MES login four weeks later.
facts.impact: About 10 hours per person per week of shadowing others instead of working, for three to five weeks.
facts.solution: Raise one access request at contract signature, so IT can prepare all accounts before day one.
facts.risks: HR has to send the request early, and accounts for people who do not start must be removed again.
facts.success_measure: Every new hire can log in on day one.

first: Die Kaffeemaschine im Pausenraum ist ständig kaputt

facts.problem: The coffee machine in the break room breaks down about once a week and stays broken for days.
facts.context: The break room of hall 2, used by about 60 people on early and late shift.
facts.evidence: It was out three times in the last four weeks; there is a note on it right now.
facts.impact: People walk to the canteen in the other building, that is about ten minutes per break.
facts.solution: Replace it with a leased machine that includes a service contract.
facts.risks: A lease costs a monthly fee from the facility budget.
facts.success_measure: No more than one day without coffee per month.

first: Night shift cannot approve a 300 euro spare part

facts.problem: When a belt breaks at night nobody on the night shift can sign the order, so the line waits for the day shift.
facts.context: Line 3, twice last month; the parts cost 200 to 400 euros and are in our budget anyway.
facts.evidence: Twice last month the line stood from about 2 am until 7:30.
facts.impact: Each stop costs about five and a half hours of production on one line.
facts.solution: Let the night shift lead approve parts orders up to 500 euros.
facts.risks: Controlling worries about orders nobody checks; a monthly review of night orders would cover that.
facts.success_measure: No line stop longer than one hour waiting for an approval.

facts.problem: The label printer at the end of line 2 jams, so boxes leave without labels and get stuck at shipping.
facts.context: Every shift, usually two or three times; it started after the new label rolls came in March.
facts.evidence: Shipping sent back 14 unlabelled boxes last week.
facts.impact: Each jam costs about 15 minutes, and every unlabelled box costs another 10 minutes at shipping.
facts.solution: Go back to the old label rolls, or have the supplier adjust the printer to the new ones.
facts.risks: The old rolls are more expensive.
facts.success_measure: Fewer than one jam per week.

first: Measurement data lives in three systems and nobody trusts it

facts.problem: Measurements are in the MES, a shared drive and two Access databases, and the numbers often disagree.
facts.context: Quality and production on the 4-series, every week when we prepare the scrap report.
facts.evidence: Last week the scrap rate was 2.1 percent in the MES and 3.4 percent in the Access file.
facts.impact: Reconciling one week costs about a full day of a quality engineer.
facts.solution: Write measurements only into the MES and retire the Access databases.
facts.risks: IT needs capacity to move the old data, and some reports read the Access files.
facts.success_measure: One scrap number per week that everybody uses.

first: Field technicians type every job sheet twice

facts.problem: Technicians fill in a paper job sheet at the customer and type it again into the system in the evening.
facts.context: All 40 field technicians, for every service job, about four jobs a day each.
facts.evidence: In my team we counted about 20 minutes of typing per evening per person.
facts.impact: About three hours per technician per week, roughly 120 hours a week for the team.
facts.solution: Offline job sheets on the tablet that sync when there is signal.
facts.risks: Some customer sites have no signal for days, so sync has to be reliable.
facts.success_measure: No more evening typing within two months of the rollout.

first: Book the endurance rig one day a week for small trials

facts.problem: Small trials never get rig time because series validation books the endurance rig six weeks ahead.
facts.context: Engineering and Line 3; four trials are waiting right now, one since June.
facts.evidence: Our belt-tension trial needs two days and has waited since June.
facts.impact: Each trial waits about six weeks; four ideas are blocked.
facts.solution: Keep Fridays on the rig for short trials, bookable the same week, as a three-month pilot.
facts.risks: Series validation loses a fifth of its rig time.
facts.success_measure: Trials start within one week of asking.
